Planned_Implementation: Vegetation treatment would occur in a mosaic pattern, leaving islands of untreated vegetation. A goal of the treatment would be to create wildlife \u201cedge\u201d on the landscape, since wildlife are known to use areas where open/shrub terrain borders tree areas. Both public lands and private lands would be treated. The following describes the preferred treatment methods, however, a variation of the treatment methods could be included in each site:\r\nIn pinyon and juniper woodland sites and sagebrush sites greater than 30% slope, selective thinning by hand cutting or mastication with machinery would be preferred. In sagebrush sites with dense pinyon and juniper cover, and less than 30% slope, chaining and mastication would be preferred. Hand thinning would occur within riparian areas. Large machinery would not be used for thinning in riparian areas. If hand thinning is used, resulting biomass would either be left onsite or piled and burned. Map 3 shows locations of the preferred treatment method for target areas.  In some areas biomass could be utilized if access is available. Biomass could take the form of ground material and chips, firewood, or posts. It is anticipated that ground material/chips and fuel wood would be the primary form of biomass utilization within the project area. Slash/biomass removal would depend on the type of vegetation treatment method used. Large trees and large tree limbs would be removed from the sites or shredded to small chips and left as mulch on the soil surface to degrade naturally. Some large trees and limbs may be left for woodcutters. The remaining slash/biomass (crushed or cut trees) would either be consolidated and burned following the treatment or left on site to degrade by natural means. Generally, the treatment area would be left open or relatively free of trees, limbs, and slash, since sage-grouse prefer open areas.\r\nPinyon and juniper trees would be selectively thinned at several small spring sources/riparian areas on public land, and at two spring sources/riparian areas on private land (Map 1). Trees would be thinned to open up the riparian areas for suitable sage-grouse habitat. Some trees would be left at these spring sources to provide shade, cover, and wildlife habitat. Most trees would be left standing along Combs Creek to provide bank stability, shade, cover, and wildlife habitat.

Objectives:
The purpose of this project was to establish a fire management experiment and demonstration
site that addressed significant local knowledge gaps hindering the management of pinyon woodland
fuels within lands managed by the BLM Bishop Field Office. The need for this information is not
unique to the Bishop Field Office, or even adjacent Inyo National Forest lands, but rather is typical of
information needed by federal, state, and other land managers throughout the Intermountain West.
Planned_Implementation: Shrubs and trees will be severed on the stump, as close to the ground as practicable, no higher than 6" from the ground. See individual unit specifications for shrub mastication requirements. All masticated vegetation will be left lying within 12&& of the ground, using a tractor with a F econ Bull Hog cutting head or equivalent. If obstacles are encountered, such as rocks or drainages, the Contractor may raise the cutter height to clear the obstacle.\r\n\r\nSpecifications for Mono Basin USGS Pinyon - 2.5-acre Sample Units (twenty-two units, 55 total acres): All live and dead pinyon pine trees shall be masticated. No leave patches in these units. The only non-masticated pinyon pines are those associated with rocky outcrops and thus are inaccessible to the equipment performing the mastication. No shrubs will be masticated, except those shrubs incidental to pinyon pine mastication. Contractor will lift head on equipment while traveling between trees.
Actual_Implementation: The mastication treatments were applied during the fall of 2006 using a Recon Bull Hog\xae masticator (figure 2 [Final Report]).
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Final Report: The cost for mastication treatment was $738 per acre, while the cut/pile/burn treatment costs
totaled $439 per acre ($339 per acre for contractors cutting and piling, plus ~$100 per acre for BLM
employees burning the piles). However, since the thinning treatments were applied on small-scale study
plots, they are not representative of typical costs. For recent management-scale mastication treatments
conducted by Bishop BLM, costs range from ~$400 per acre for low tree encroachment, ~$600 per
acres for moderate tree encroachment, and ~$800–1000 per acre for high tree encroachment.
Management-scale cut/pile/burn treatment costs range from ~$150 per acre for low tree encroachment,
~$350 per acre for moderate tree encroachment, and ~$600 per acre for high tree encroachment for the
cutting and piling, plus ~$60 per acre for burning. BLM’s planning costs are not included in these
estimates; however, planning effort is similar for the different thinning techniques and levels of tree
encroachment.

MANAGEMENT IMPLICATIONS
Thinning Approaches
Both thinning treatments were equally effective at reducing the target fuels which were mature,
live pinyon trees. Application costs though differed substantially, with the cut/pile/burn technique much
cheaper even though that technique required chain saw crews consisting of multiple people as opposed
to a masticator operated by a single individual.
Vegetation Responses
In general, thinning treatments stimulated the abundance of herbaceous vegetation, although in
some cases the strength of the stimulation appeared to be constrained by the level of pre-treatment tree
encroachment. Increases in perennial grass cover and density in response to thinning were usually
greatest at lower levels of pre-treatment pinyon dominance, while native annual forb density and cover
responded fairly equally along the tree-dominance gradient. The rapid recovery of annual forb
vegetation in sites with high pinyon abundance didn’t appear to be constrained by a lack of seed source,
which is a particular concern for managers when applying treatments within highly tree-encroached
shrublands. However, our findings suggest a lack of adequate seed sources and/or existing individuals
appears to be limiting the initial response of perennial grasses in areas with high tree encroachment. At
the higher levels of tree dominance, perennial grass cover within the thinning treatments did start to
exceed the control by 3 years post-treatment, while perennial grass density was still similar or slightly
lower than the controls. This seems to suggest that the thinning-induced increase in perennial grass
cover within areas of high tree dominance is mainly due to an increase in growth of individuals present
prior to the treatment, as opposed to an increase due to the recruitment of new individuals.

Shrub abundance exhibited a steep decline in response to tree encroachment and the response to
thinning treatments appeared more subtle. Shrub cover within the control decreased slightly during the
3 post-treatment years, while it increased slightly within both thinning treatment. The response of
slower-growing plants such as shrubs will need to be evaluated during future years to determine
differences between thinning treatments.
Species richness within the two thinning treatments steadily increased relative to the control over
the course of the 3 years following treatment, and the response was similar in both thinning treatments.
Species richness was also consistent across the pinyon-dominance gradient, which suggests that the
ability for vegetation to recover at this location may not be significantly limited by a lack of seed
availability or lack of species diversity within highly tree-encroached shrublands. At this location, the
distances between phase very low and very high tree-encroached areas are on the order of 100s of
meters, which may not be enough to limit seed dispersal into areas of high tree cover.
Fuel-bed Responses
Both thinning treatments equally affected the target fuels, standing live pinyon trees. The cover
of herbaceous live fuels (perennial and annual forbs and grasses) and live woody fuels (live shrubs and
trees) were also similar between the two thinning treatments and higher than the control. The greatest
difference in fuel structure between the two fuel treatments appeared to be dead woody fuel loads—
mastication clearly resulted in greater fine fuel loads (1–100 hour fuels) as well as the shredded woody
particles. The stimulation of live herbaceous cover—especially at lower pre-treatment pinyon
dominance—may have important implications for fire spread by enhancing the continuity of surface
fuels, especially during dry years.

Objectives:
The purpose of the Proposed Action is to reduce hazardous fuels on BLM land in Antelope
Valley. Many of the areas proposed for treatment are immediately adjacent to homes and
communities in Antelope Valley. In these cases, the proposed treatments are intended to
decrease the intensity of future wildland fires in the treated areas, and increase the safety of
residents, private property, and firefighters working to protect the community and suppress
fires.
Planned_Implementation:
Brush can be either mowed or hand-cut. Mowing shall be done with low ground
pressure (less than 6 psi) rubber-tracked or rubber-tired equipment, (such as an ASV or
Bobcat) equipped with a mowing head capable of mowing brush up to 8 feet tall.
Contractor shall mow all areas within each unit, except for flagged exclusion areas and
other areas deemed unsafe for mowing (rocky outcrops, short stretches of steep slope,
etc. ... ). Mower head shall be set to leave a stubble height of 6 to 9 inches. The
Contractor's operations shall be conducted carefully to minimize soil disturbance by the
equipment. Where excessive slope, rocky terrain, or other factors prevent the use of
mowing equipment, brush cutting by hand with chainsaws or similar equipment will be
required. Material generated from hand cutting operations will be either moved within
the treatment unit to a location where the mowing equipment can treat it, or hand-fed
into a chipper.

The Contractor will leave occasional shrubs un-mowed to improve visual appearance of
project. Smaller (less than 18 inches in height) bitterbrush and sagebrush are preferred
as leave shrubs. Shrubs should be randomly left, with 40 to SO feet the average spacing
between shrubs.

Trt_Concerns_Desc: A combination of 100 years of fire suppression and past livestock grazing practices have allowed the pinyon/juniper woodland to increase its range and expand into areas historically dominated by sagebrush and perennial grasses. In the  project area remaining shrub lands are dominated by homogenous stands of mature sagebrush with declining, remnant populations of native perennial forbs and grasses. Much of the ground below the pinyon/juniper closed canopy has little or no shrubs, forbs or grasses, all of which are important to wildlife, livestock and ecosystem stability. The sagebrush corridors that once connected the Bald Hills and the Greenville Bench, and facilitated the movement and dispersal of sagebrush obligate species such as sage grouse, have disappeared due to pinyon/ juniper encroachment. Due to the current condition of the watershed, a catastrophic wildfire would cause large-scale damage to the watershed and would be very hard to control.\r\n   The following actions have been identified by resource and fire management professionals as necessary on the Greenville Bench area: 1) establishing fuel breaks along selected roads, property lines and topographic features on the lower sagebrush bench creating a situation where wildfires can be better managed by reducing the rate of spread and giving fire fighters additional response time to suppress fires&* 2) decreasing the hazardous fuel loads on the mid and upper slopes in the pinyon/juniper woodland, thereby protecting against the threat of catastrophic wildfires leaving the woodlands and impacting neighboring private lands and Interstate 15&* 3) re-establishing sagebrush corridors between the Bald Hills and the Greenville Bench allowing for better dispersal and movement of wildlife species&* 4) decreasing the amount of pinyon/juniper encroachment into areas historically dominated by big sagebrush&* 5) increasing plant diversity within the treatment areas by establishing a mix of native and non-native shrubs, forbs and grasses that would also facilitate a decrease in surface soil erosion as a result of precipitation and wind&* 6) improve the health of both woodlands and sagebrush/grasslands by increasing biological diversity and age class.

Trt_Concerns_Desc: The purpose of the proposal is to return the Kern Mountain landscape to a Fire Regime Condition Class 1. Fire Regime Condition Class (FRCC) is an interagency, standardized tool based on scientific and peer reviewed literature for determining the degree of departure from reference condition vegetation, fuels and disturbance regimes (http://www.frcc.gov/). Assessing FRCC can help guide management objectives and set priorities for treatments. The classification is based on a relative measure describing the degree of departure from the historical natural disturbance regime. This departure is described as changes to one or more of the following ecological components: vegetation characteristics (species composition, structural stages, stand age, canopy closure and mosaic pattern)&* fuel composition&* fire frequency, severity and pattern&* and other associated disturbances (e.g. insects and disease mortality, grazing and drought). The three classes are based on low (0-33% departure&* FRCC1), moderate (34-66% departure&* FRCC2) and high (67-100% departure&* FRCC3) departure from central tendency of the natural (historical) regime. Low departure is considered to be within the natural (historical) range of variability, while moderate and high departures are outside the range of variability. The FRCC rating is accompanied by a series of indicators of the potential risks that may result from the changes to the associated ecological components when disturbance is applied. Reference descriptions for a typical FRCC 1 community have been developed for most major vegetation types. Reference conditions are compared to actual (on the ground) conditions for purposes of determining current FRCC classes. The need for the proposal is to respond to the high departure from natural conditions in the area due to a combination of drought, fire suppression efforts and historic livestock overgrazing. The majority of the project area is rated FRCC 3 (highly departed). Current FRCC (Fire Regime Condition Class) data for lower elevations of the Kern Mountains indicates the area has been missing the necessary fire return intervals to sustain ecosystem health. The lack of fire has produced an overgrowth of shrub species in the area historically dominated by native grasses. This overgrowth further threatens the ecologically stability of the Kern Mountains and the ability of firefighting forces to control unwanted high to extreme fire perturbations. The use of fire as a tool to alter fuel loadings and re-establish fire as a more common occurrence is necessary for ecological stability.

Treatment_Type: Tree/Brush Control: Pinyon Juniper Removal - Hand Cutting
Objectives: The purposes of the project are to : 1)  Create a strategically located fuelbreak between two distinct areas of the Pine Nut Mountains; 2)  Reduce the threat of wildfire damage to critical sage grouse habitat; and 3)  Enhance sage grouse habitat.\r\nTreatment Objective:  Modify the structure, amount and continuity of pinyon and juniper trees within the treatment area in order to reduce fire intensity and restore sage grouse habitat.
Planned_Implementation:
Treatment Activities  The total treatment area would be up to 2,550 acres.  Treatments would include a combination of the following:

Tree Cutting and Partial Tree Removal - Pinyon and juniper trees would be cut with hand tools and small mechanized tools and a portion of the trees removed for firewood, either personal use or commercial sale.  Firewood cutting treatment areas would be identified away from sage  grouse leks, where larger trees are present and located near existing roads (see project map).  Vegetation remnants (slash) would be left in place and shredded by subsequent mechanical shredding operations.  Firewood cutting activities would be terminated prior to initiation of shredding operations within areas scheduled for shredding.  Treatment size: up to 62 acres.

Tree Cutting and No Removal - Pinyon and juniper trees would be cut and lopped and scattered on site.  Cut, lop and scatter treatment areas would be where trees are small and sparse and/or where topography or rock limits the use of mechanized equipment.  Stump height would be less than 6 inches and slash height would not exceed 3 feet in depth.  Treatment size: up to 1000 acres.
 
Mechanical Tree Shredding - Rubber tired/tracked or metal tracked mechanized equipment with a mastication head would be used to shred trees.  All pinyon and juniper trees within the treatment area would be targeted for shredding except for small pockets identified for avoidance to protect sensitive resources.  The shrub community would not be targeted for shredding but would be thinned indirectly as part of the tree shredding process.  Slash left behind from tree cutting and partial tree removal would be shredded.  Stump height would be less than 6 inches and the products of shredding would not exceed 2 feet in depth. Shredded vegetation would be left in place to reduce wind generation of dust and stabilize the soil surface.  Treatment size:  up to 2,100 acres. 

Full Tree Removal - Rubber tired/tracked or metal tracked mechanized equipment would be used to shear, either skid or above ground haul, and chip pinyon pine and juniper trees.  All pinyon and juniper trees within the treatment area would be targeted for shredding except for small pockets identified for avoidance to protect sensitive resources.   Shearing would include separating the tree from the stump, less than 6 inches from the ground.  Once the trees are sheared, they would be skidded or hauled to a designated landing or processing area.  The trees would then be chipped and hauled off site.  Treatment size:  up to 2,100 acres.
Actual_Implementation: Lop and scatter was completed.  Summitt Forests were efficient, professional and economical.  The production rate was about 4 acres per person per day.  The contract was awarded at $164 per acre.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results: All objectives are currently being met. Cheatgrass is present in the project area but is not the dominant grass species by any means. It appears that the understory is intact and this project was taken from R-3 to R-0.

Trt_Concerns_Desc: The proposed project is located in a north-south trending valley between two mountainous and heavily forested areas of the Pine Nut Mountains.  Singleleaf pinyon pine and Utah juniper trees dominate the mountain slopes as well as the majority of the project area.  Fuels in these areas are heavy and would support an intense wildfire under the hot windy conditions common during the summer months.  \r\n   The potential plant community in the project area is mainly sagebrush, bitterbrush and perennial grasses (Soil Survey of Lyon County Area, Nevada, 1984).  Pinyon and juniper trees, in the proposed project area, are in the process of forming a horizontally continuous bed of heavy fuels between the mountainous forested areas.  If this situation is not addressed fuel loads would increase, understory vegetation would be stressed and depleted, and the stage would be set for a widespread destructive high intensity wildfire.  Such a wildfire would be difficult and dangerous to control and could destroy near-by sage grouse habitat including a lek and seasonal habitat.\r\n   One of the few known active sage grouse leks in the Northern Pine Nut Mountains is located less than 2 miles from the northeastern edge of the project.  The majority of the project area ranges from 2 to 6 miles from the lek.  Areas this distance from a lek often are utilized by sage grouse for a variety of purposes such as nesting, brooding, migration corridors and other seasonal uses.  High quality habitat adjacent to leks is needed to support viable sage grouse populations.  Encroachment of pinyon and juniper trees into the shrub community, have degraded sage grouse habitat quality in the project area.  Thinning and/or removal of the trees combined with restoration of the understory vegetation community would improve habitat quality.

Objectives: The goal of the Rosette project is to manage the existing fire risk to the Rosette community by reducing the amount of continuous fuels ( cheatgrass, sagebrush, and greasewood) in order to lessen the potential damage or severity/intensity of wildland fire. We hope to lessen the speed and severity of wildland fires, that may occur in this area and threaten nearby developments, by increasing the diversity of the vegetative community and breaking up the monocultures that now exist within the project area. As stated in the proposed plan for this project, our objectives are to: (1) reduce the average canopy cover of sagebrush to equal 15-25% and increase the combined forb and perennial grass average canopy cover to equal 20-25%, (2) reduce sagebrush and greasewood in a mosaic pattern (following the natural contours of the landscape) on 20-\r\n60% of the total project area. This will help to reduce the risk of extreme fire behavior in the area, and protect the Rosette community and adjacent properties from being threatened by such fire behavior. It will also help to increase the diversity of vegetation within the area and introduce age-class and size-class diversity in the sagebrush and greasewood community.
Planned_Implementation: A tractor/dozer would pull a brush cruncher (pasture aerator) that would crush, tear, and chop older stagnate age classes of sagebrush allowing younger, supple age classes to spring back with little or no harm. The abundant deep-rooted greasewood would be disced and then may be followed by a cultipacker to compact the soil if needed. A seeding treatment would occur by attaching a drop seeder to the back of the brush cruncher with a less flammable seed species (see Seed Species List, Appendix 1 ).

All live and standing dead trees exceeding 1 foot in total height within identified
treatment unit boundaries shall be completely severed from the stump. No live
branches shall be left on the stump of cut trees. Stumps must not exceed, on the side
adjacent to the highest ground, a maximum height of 6 inches for stumps 12 inches in
diameter and larger or a maximum height of 4 inches for stumps less than 12 inches in
diameter.

Cut trees shall be limbed and bucked to facilitate piling and/or scattering. Limbs and
stems shall be bucked so as not to exceed six feet in total length. All Contractor generated
tree material and all pre-existing down and dead tree material shall be hand
piled or scattered per the following specifications:
Cut tress less than 10 feet in height and less than 6 inches in diameter at the base that
are greater than 100 feet from any other trees in the unit must be loped and scattered.

Limbs shall be scattered into natural openings on the ground and far enough apart to
avoid piling.

Cut tress greater than 10 feet in height and/or greater than 6 inches in diameter at the
base must be piled. Cut tree less than 10 feet in height and less than 6 inches in
diameter at the base that are within 100 feet of other trees in the unit must also be
piled. Hand piles shall be constructed in a tight, compact fashion and to a height of not

The purpose of the proposed action is to improve and maintain habitat conditions for Greater Sage-Grouse (Centrocercus urophasianus) and other sagebrush associated wildlife species in the vicinity of the Stringer Meadow (Lek 9) and Lower Summers Meadow (Lek 10) leks in Mono County, California.

The proposed action was developed and designed to address the following sage-grouse conservation objectives identified by the Bodie PMU local working group: 1) Improve sage-grouse habitat quality by treating pinyon and/or juniper encroachment into key sage-grouse habitats in the Bodie PMU&* and 2) Manage pinyon and juniper in the Bodie PMU to ensure long-term connectivity between sage-grouse seasonal use areas and adjacent breeding populations (NDOW 2004, Appendix L, p. 96).

In 2007, the BLM Bishop Field Office entered into a cooperative agreement with The Nature Conservancy (TNC) to develop a Conservation Action Plan (CAP) for the Bodie Hills. The purpose of the CAP was to inform and guide the formulation of future site-specific vegetation management strategies to protect and enhance the area’s ecological integrity. As part of the CAP process, a combination of remote sensing, field surveys, and ecological modeling was used to evaluate the current condition of ecological systems in the Bodie Hills as compared to their predicted natural range of variability. The results of this analysis indicate that montane sagebrush steppe, Wyoming big sagebrush, and basin big sagebrush ecosystems in the Bodie Hills are currently “highly departed” from their natural range of variability. The analysis also indicated that low sagebrush ecosystems in the Bodie Hills are “moderately departed” from their natural range of variability. The CAP analysis identified the over representation of mid seral (Class C), late seral (Class E), and uncharacteristic (Class U) ecological classes in these ecosystems as primary contributors to this departure. Chainsaw lopping and canopy thinning of conifer trees and prescribed fire are among the recommended management strategies for restoring these ecosystems (Provencher et al. 2009).

Trt_Concerns_Desc:
Recent research in the Great Basin has demonstrated clearly that pinyon and juniper are
increasing in density throughout much of this region and many areas that were formerly
dominated by shrubs are now being taken over by pin yon and juniper (Rom me et al. 2002, GL TI
1997, Naillon 1999, West et al. 1987). The Salt Lake Field Office is experiencing encroachment
of Utah juniper (Juniperus Osteosperma) between the Simpson and Sheeprock Mountains&*
beyond its historic densities. This process is creating a tree over story which decreases the
climax shrub and grass species due to shading and increased water resource competition. When
juniper canopy cover increases, the potential for crown fire activity becomes greater due to the
extra fuel loading available. Crown fires in thick juniper stands are difficult and expensive to
suppress and exhibit greater severity to the vegetation and soils. The current hazardous fuel
conditions within the area are at risk for unusually large and severe wildfires. Although some
native understory still exists, it is being out competed by juniper and is at risk of conversion to
juniper woodland barring any disturbance or to cheatgrass following wildfire.
In this light, it is evident that a hazardous fuels treatment is needed in order to begin the process
of restoring the integrity of the sagebrush steppe and reduce the potential for large, devastating
wildfires.

The Stonehouse hazardous fuels reduction and habitat improvement project is an ongoing project with multiple actions. The project consists of two way chaining, hand thinning, mowing, drill seeding and potential mastication. The total project area consists of 23,676 acres of which up to 19,000 acres may be treated. Presently the first phase of the chaining (approximately 4,000 acres) has been initiated. The second phase of the chaining may consist of up to 2,284 acres, mowing and drill seeding areas may consist of up to 2,500 acres, mastication and hand thinning may be used to treat the remaining acres. The action is designed to improve sagebrush habitat within the North Spring Valley area and to remove encroaching trees from sage grouse leking and brooding habitat.  The objectives for the proposed action are to:
• Reduce late seral and decadent sagebrush stands within the treatment area, to recruit younger more vigorous sagebrush and increase the herbaceous understory.
• Provide additional water sources as deemed necessary through consultation with the Nevada Division of Wildlife to support and improve populations of big game and small game within North Spring Valley.
• Increase the amount of time available for project implementation to accommodate the availability of resources and environmental factors such as weather and soils conditions.

largely by dense juniper (Juniperus osteosperma). This area fit into the Hazardous fuels

The proposal is to conduct maintenance on the Woods McCullough, Burnt Canyon, and Reeds
Cabin Habitat Improvement Projects. These habitat improvement projects were
completed in 1996 for Woods McCullough, 1976 for Burnt Canyon, and 1993 for Reeds Cabin
using mechanical methods to remove the pinyon and juniper trees. Total project area is
approximately 3,226 acres in three locations&* the Woods McCullough project (1 ,046 acres), the
Burnt Canyon project (1 ,604 acres) and the Reeds Cabin project (576 acres). Maintenance of
these projects would consist of hand crews using chain saws to cut the regenerating pinyon and
juniper trees within the previously treated areas. Slash from the cutting would be scattered in
areas with fewer trees and then piled in areas with thicker trees. Piles would be a maximum of 5
feet by 5 feet by 5 feet in size. The majority of these piled would then be disposed of through
prescribed burning. The remaining piles would be left for small game habitat. Prescribed
burning would take place during the winter when there is snow on the ground and/or following a
precipitation event. Project implementation would begin in 2010 and
proceed as funding is available until completed.

Objectives: The short-term (within one year of project\r\nimplementation) objectives of the project are: 1) reduce sagebrush cover of decadent and old sagebrush cover by at least 50%, 2) improve vigor of sagebrush plants, and 3) create a mosaic fuelbreak that could be used to control a wildfire. The long-term objectives for the project are: 1) Increase the percent composition by weight (Ibs/acre) of perennial grasses and forbs to a minimum of 65% of the ecological site potential within ten years following completion of the treatment.
Planned_Implementation: The proposed action is to mow approximately 1,000 acres of Wyoming big sagebrush habitat in southern Garden Valley. Sagebrush would be mowed to a height of approximately three to six inches above ground level. The treatment would be conducted through the use of a rubber wheeled tractor pulling a twenty-foot wide sagebrush mower. Treatments would be conducted in a mosaic pattern that would leave irregular boundaries and islands within the treatment polygon.
Actual_Implementation: Mowing of 996 acres completed. Implementation verified by GIS attribute table. John Uhalde and Co. provided tractor and labor. BLM paid for brush mower and parts for mower, NEPA documentation, cultural clearances, monitoring, and other surveys, etc.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
The project site indicated excellent response to the mowing treatment. The removal of the decadent sagebrush plants resulted in the establishment of healthy, native plants with a diverse mixture of grasses, forbs and shrubs. The vegetation displayed excellent health, vigor and production in comparison to the adjacent untreated areas. The recruitment of young, healthy native plants was evident. The primary species present included Wyoming big sagebrush, galleta, bottlebrush squirreltail and globemallow. Other species present included Indian ricegrass, needle and thread and rabbitbrush. There were minimal to no non-native, invasive species present. There were a few cheatgrass and mustard plants present. Overall, the project area displayed a healthy, vigorous native plant community. The progress and improvement in the plant community was excellent considering that the treatment was only completed one year prior to the monitoring study being conducted.

Overall, the total overall canopy cover increased in 2013 from the 2009 monitoring event. Overall perennial grass cover nearly doubled from 12.5% (12% - 13%) in 2009 to 24% (20% - 28%) in 2013 and density remained unchanged with an average of 74,869 plants/acre for both 2009 (43106 – 106631 plants/acre) and 2013 (70332 – 79406 plants/acre). Overall shrub cover increased slightly from 5% (5% - 5%) in 2009 to 8.5% (5% - 12%) in 2013 and density increased slightly from an average of 5,105 plants/acre in 2009 (3403 – 4538 plants/acre) to 7,374 plants/acre in 2013 (3403 – 11344 plants/acre) which was a result of an increase in sagebrush canopy cover and density. Overall forb cover decreased from 7% (5% - 9%) in 2009 to 0.5% (0 – 1%) in 2013 and density of perennial forbs decreased from 6,239 plants/acre (3403 – 9075 plants/acre) in 2009 to 5,672 plants/acre (0-11344 plants/acre) in 2013. Cheatgrass cover increased dramatically from 0% in 2009 to 13% (10% - 15%) in 2013 and density increased from 0 plants/acre in 2009 to 263,742 plants/acre (106631 – 420853 plant/acre) in 2013. 2009 was a relatively wet year, particularly the spring and early summer, which resulted in very high production of forbs. The winter/spring precipitation for 2013 was relatively low and temperature warmed quickly. This may explain some of the variability in forb production. 
The vegetation still appeared to be vigorous and productive, particularly the sagebrush and galleta grass, both of which had long leader growth and seed stocks and appeared to have good seed production for the year for galleta and appeared that it may be good for sagebrush. Most of the vegetation had already or was close to dormancy for the summer due to the lack of precipitation and warm weather.

SHORT TERM GOAL 	SUCCES:
Reduce decadent sagebrush cover by at least 50 percent.    N/A
Improve vigor of sagebrush plants.      YES
Create a mosaic fuel break for wildfire control.      YES
Increase relative cover of desirable, perennial herbaceous species by 10 percent.     YES

LONG TERM GOAL 	SUCCES:
Increase the percent composition by weight (lbs/acre) of perennial grasses and forbs to a minimum of 65 percent of the ecological site potential within ten years following completion of the treatment.          N/A
Note: There appears to be significant progress being made towards meeting the above long term goal based on the vegetative response only one year following completion of the treatment.

Trt_Concerns_Desc:
The primary purpose of the Proposed Action is to improve availability, quantity, and quality of sagebrush, woodland, and wet meadow/riparian habitats that multiple wildlife species, wild horses, and livestock depend on.

The first need is to restore and enhance degraded sage-grouse habitat stemming from pinyon/juniper (PJ) expansion into sagebrush and quality brood rearing habitats and/or excessive horse use. Healthy, resilient springs/wet meadows support abundant and diverse forb and insect populations. Sage-grouse chicks are critically dependent on the protein for survival, and in turn, recruitment into breeding-capable adults. In particular, wet meadows in Dalton Canyon are degraded from PJ expansion coupled with heavy wild horse use, as well as permitted livestock grazing use of meadows, and a wet meadow in Porter Canyon is degraded from PJ expansion. This has changed the hydrology that in turn has led to decreased plant diversity and declining sage-grouse use.

The second need is to decrease density of PJ that has been identified as a primary factor in mule deer population declines as well as several woodland dependent bird species. Mule deer, pinyon jays, mountain chickadees, and scrub jays depend on woodland landscapes that have a more open canopy and park-like structure with a robust understory of forbs, grasses, and shrubs. In highly dense PJ stands, the understory has been eliminated or is in decline. Increasing density and encroachment is also degrading springs/wet meadows in mule deer habitat and aspen stands in riparian areas.

The third need is to reduce the high fire risk stemming from increased PJ density and to restore a cheatgrass dominated landscape near Cold Springs that has resulted from previous fires. The Fire Regime Condition Class (FRCC) is a numerical rating representing the degree of departure from the historical fire regime and vegetation conditions, or in other words, fire frequency and severity.

Trt_Concerns_Desc:
Studies show that the expansion of pinyon-juniper has more than tripled in the areas dominated by pinyon-juniper woodlands within the last 150 years. Although pinyon and juniper woodlands have increased dramatically in the last 150 years, they currently occupy far less than they are capable of under current climatic conditions (Miller & Tausch, 2001). These changes have generally coincided with the introduction of heavy livestock grazing, tree utilization by the mining industry, and fire suppression that followed settlement of the region. An increase in tree dominance results in a loss of understory. A loss of understory further reduces the fuel and further decreases the fire frequency. Altered disturbance regimes and climate change have resulted in major changes in plant community compositions. Since the 1860’s, many bunchgrass and sagebrush-bunchgrass communities, which dominated the Intermountain West, have shifted to pinyon and juniper woodland or introduced annual-dominated communities (West 1984, Miller
et al. 1994). Studies conclude that barring some major environmental change or management action, continued forage reduction and decreased fire frequency will continue until trees dominate most of the sites favorable to their survival. This continued tree dominance then jeopardizes the historic woodland sites because under the right conditions, a crown fire could result in a stand replacement wildfire with catastrophic consequences because of continuous tree canopy. Studies further show that in pinyon-juniper communities that are overstocked, the ability of the understory to respond after a fire is dramatically reduced and potentially opens the site to the invasion by exotics.

The need for action is to:
● Reverse expansion of pinyon-juniper woodlands because of the negative effects on wildlife
habitat quality.
● Prevent large-scale wildland fire resulting from the buildup of fuels and the conversion of fuel
type based on prediction from historic assessments.
● Improve species composition and diversity.
● Reverse the decreasing quality of wildlife habitat and forage due to damage from wildfires.
● Prevent the establishment and expansion of invasive non-native species.

Objectives: Mastication of pinyon-juniper in conjunction with seeding treatment to allow for growth of understory and habitat improvement.
Planned_Implementation:
The contractor will be required to remove all live pinyon and juniper trees, standing skeletons and snags of dead pinyon and juniper trees, as well as all recent blow down trees through the means of mastication.

Work specifications applicable to the project area are as follows:
• Sever and masticate all pinyon and juniper trees within the project area not identified as leave trees. If obstacles are encountered (i.e. large rocks) during treatment, the mastication attachment may be raised to clear the obstacle.
• Mulch, being the bi-product of mechanical mastication, will not cover the ground to a depth of greater than 6 inches, and no residual piece of mulch shall be greater than two feet in length or 4 inches in diameter. All stumps shall be ground so they are no greater than 6 inches in height on the uphill side above mineral soil.
• Implementation will terminate in the event wet conditions arise and the ground is saturated where equipment is causing excessive rutting (>3 inches) and disturbance. Work can resume when the ground is sufficiently dry and with the concurrence of the government.
• Operators of equipment will make every attempt to take different paths to and from the base camp to work area in order to limit the amount of disturbance upon a single path. In the event a single path is utilized to the extent that it resembles a road, it is the responsibility of the contractor to implement reclamation of the disturbance to a state resembling the rest of the treatment.
• Trees containing raptor nests discovered during project implementation shall be retained.
• All mountain mahogany trees will be left untreated.
• Active mining claim markers or stakes shall be avoided. Active mining claim markers that are destroyed by operations would be the Contractors responsibility to re-stake using a legal mining claim marker. The re-staking of mining claim markers would occur in coordination with the existing mining claimants to ensure accurate, legal staking procedures that would minimize damage to claims.
• All Contract equipment will be inspected by the Government or designated Project Inspector prior to equipment being offloaded from its transport. The inspection location needs to be pre-arranged to best serve both contractor and government representatives.
Actual_Implementation: Mastication (grinding) completed, verified by GIS attribute table and As-Built treatment map.

Since the 1860’s, many bunchgrass and sagebrush-bunchgrass communities, which dominated the Intermountain West, have shifted to pinyon and juniper woodland or introduced annual-dominated communities (West 1984, Miller
et al. 1994). Studies conclude that barring some major environmental change or management action, continued forage reduction and decreased fire frequency will continue until trees dominate most of the sites favorable to their survival. This continued tree dominance then jeopardizes the historic woodland sites because under the right conditions, a crown fire could result in a stand replacement wildfire with catastrophic consequences because of continuous tree canopy. Studies further show that in pinyon-juniper communities that are overstocked, the ability of the understory to respond after a fire is dramatically reduced and potentially opens the site to the invasion by exotics.

The need for action is to:
● Reverse expansion of pinyon-juniper woodlands because of the negative effects on wildlife
habitat quality.
● Prevent large-scale wildland fire resulting from the buildup of fuels and the conversion of fuel
type based on prediction from historic assessments.
● Improve species composition and diversity.
● Reverse the decreasing quality of wildlife habitat and forage due to damage from wildfires.
● Prevent the establishment and expansion of invasive non-native species.

Objectives: Native communities can only be reestablished if the density of pinyon and juniper is  reduced and desired native species have an adequate seed bank or are seeded. Changes in\r\ntree density can range from near complete stand removal to limited thinning. Chaining and other mechanical treatments are substitutes to natural tree control most frequently attained by wildfires. The objectives of most improvement projects should not be to remove all trees, but to remove sufficient numbers to allow recovery of the understory species and to facilitate artificial seeding.
Planned_Implementation:
The Contractor is expected to modify approximately 95 percent of the structure, amount and continuity of the pinyon and juniper trees through mechanical grinding in order to reduce fire intensity potential and improve ecosystem health. Trees will be severed on the stump, no higher than six inches above the ground and treated to lie within 12 inches of the ground. The product of grinding will be a mulch layer less than 12 inches deep, consisting of material less than 3 feet in length and 4 inches in diameter. 
Tree spacing will be adjusted to approximately 80 feet between individual trees or groups of trees. Tree thinning will target smaller diameter trees, retaining primarily larger Pinyon pine trees. All Mountain mahogany trees will be retained. Patches of brush and trees varying in size and spacing will be identified by the government and left untreated. Where applicable trees will be retained in small groups with openings between the groups. Areas with healthy shrubs and grasses will be the target locations for openings. 
Shrubs and trees will be severed on the stump, no higher than six inches above the ground and treated to lie within 12 inches of the ground. 

	Trees containing raptor nests discovered during project implementation will be retained 	If obstacles are encountered, such as rocks, the Contractor may raise the cutter height to clear the obstacle. Implementation will be limited to daylight hours.
Actual_Implementation: The mastication contract was completed, verified by record of completion, GIS attribute table, and contract invoice.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Coyote East Mastication Summary (2015) - Overall, foliar cover was estimated at 30.75% for the masticated and aerially seeded area. Shrub cover was the largest component of foliar cover, with 23.25% average cover consisting mostly of rabbitbrush (Chyrsothamnun visidiflorus sbsp. Visidiflorus) and black sage (Artemesia nova) as well as some horsebrush (Tetradymia canescans). Perennial grasses, both existing growth and seeded species comprise 5.75% of estimate foliar cover. Bareground comprised 14.75% of the area, less prevalent than in the chaining areas. Litter however was less common with only 13.25% cover.

Density survey results revealed three seeded species. Basin wildrye was observed at 0.25 per meter squared, Sainfoin at 0.25 per meter squared, and Snake river wheatgrass at half a meter squared. However, seeded small burnet, arrowleaf balsamroot, and Indian ricegrass were also observed in the monitoring plot and the seeding area.

Species richness and diversity was very high for the site - twenty four different species were recorded.

Mule deer scat was observed but no grazing was seen by mule deer or any other ungulate species. Invasive plants, including cheatgrass, were observed with <1% cover in the area.


Recommendations - Due to the need to further establish more seed species it is recommended that the project area remained closed to cattle grazing for at least two more growing season in order for seeded perennial bunchgrasses, forbs, and shrubs to establish.

Trt_Concerns_Desc: Fuel breaks are strategically located wide blocks or strips of land in which vegetation of lower fuel volume or flammability is managed to aid in the control of wildfires, thus reducing the risk of catastrophic wildfire.  Maintaining fuel volume and/or fire-resistant vegetation will help protect surrounding areas at risk of damage from wildfire.  The purpose of this fuel break is to protect big game habitat, specifically critical deer winter range. Currently large areas of continuous mature sagebrush occupy the treatment area. Once constructed, the fuel break would be maintained under the BLM hazardous fuels program by using mechanical or biological means when determined necessary through on-going monitoring of fuel loadings in the treatment area.
